html:
The campaign of the pharaoh Thutmose I around 1504 BCE that pushed Egyptian power far up the Nile into Nubia, beyond the Third Cataract, and broke the kingdom of Kerma.

Kerma, in today's Sudan, had been a rich and powerful state, and during the troubled years before the New Kingdom it had even raided Egypt. Thutmose struck back. He reached a point beyond the Fourth Cataract, where he left an inscription, and sacked Kerma. His grandson Thutmose III finished the conquest.

Egypt ruled Nubia, which it called Kush, for some four centuries. A viceroy, the King's Son of Kush, governed it, and it supplied gold, ivory, ebony, cattle and soldiers. The Egyptians built temples there, including a great one to Amun at Gebel Barkal, and the Nubian elite took up Egyptian gods and writing.

When Egypt pulled back around 1070 BCE, a new Kushite kingdom grew around Napata. It kept the cult of Amun, and its kings came back north to rule Egypt themselves: see Piye of Kush conquers Egypt and Kush.
sum: The campaign of the pharaoh Thutmose I around 1504 BCE that pushed Egyptian power far up the Nile into Nubia, beyond the Third Cataract, and broke the kingdom of Kerma.
